title: Probe-led scheduler autotune scrapbook
content:
Status: working notebook / field notes. High-level: exploring a light-weight probe-based autotuner that nudges batching timeouts and probe sizes toward a target tail (p99/p995) while preserving fairness across customer tiers. This doc captures the experiments we ran 08/14–09/02, the telemetry we collected, micro-profiling breadcrumbs, and early heuristics we think are promising.

Why a prober?
- Continuous batching has many local minima: fixed timeouts either hurt tail or throughput depending on traffic mix.
- We want an adaptive controller that: (a) minimally perturbs steady-state throughput, (b) detects shifts in request length distribution, (c) reacts to tail spikes without oscillation, (d) enforces simple fairness constraints.

Design summary (short):
- Runner: lightweight probe tasks emitted at small fraction f of requests (configurable by service tier). Probes carry synthetic short/long tokens to exercise latency-critical paths.
- Signals: p50/p90/p99/p995 latency, batch formation sizes, queue occupancy, kernel-time percent (CUDA kernels), scheduler preemption count, KV-cache hit ratio.
- Control knobs: base_timeout_ms, extra_timeout_on_probe_ms, max_batch_size, probe_fraction, probe_payload_profile.
- Objective: drive p995 for tier X to <= target_ms with minimal throughput loss and with no more than 5% drop in fairness_score (see below).

Experiment harness (setup):
- Target machine: a4-48 (8xA100 analog), runtime image rwd-runtime:v3.2.1, quantized LLM v2.1 (8-bit), batcher=continuous-batcher-v1
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes: steady-short (mostly <64 tokens), mixed (power-law length distribution mean 128), skewed-long (heavy tail, 5% >1024 tokens). We also replayed traces from customer A (anonymized) for 24h to validate generalization.
- Measurement window: sliding 5m windows, aggregated every 30s. Probes: probe_fraction values swept {0.1%, 0.5%, 1%}. Probe payloads: short (prompt <32), long (prefix 512 tokens), and tail-probe (simulate multi-continue generation to exercise KV cache).

Important instrumentation notes:
- Enabled kernel-level tracing for a subset of runs (NVIDIA Nsight sampling) to capture kernel duration distribution. Observed heavy skew to a single fused attention kernel for long-service requests.
- Added lightweight counters inside batcher to emit distribution of batch sizes per flush and age histogram for oldest request in flush.
- Hooked scheduler trace id into our flamegraph pipeline; links in linked_artifacts point to representative traces.

Key findings (summary):
1) Probe fraction 0.5% is a good tradeoff: detects tail regime changes within ~90s while adding <0.8% throughput overhead. 0.1% was noisy; 1% increased throughput cost noticeably for mixed workloads.
2) Using a small extra_timeout_on_probe_ms (20–40ms) allowed the controller to measure what additional waiting would yield in batch size improvements without affecting user-facing timeouts. This gave a clearer gradient for autotune decisions.
3) Kernel hotspot: when probes indicated higher p99, the profiler showed increased memcpy and attention kernel time. Hypothesis: long requests were causing kernel-launch contention and L2 thrash on multi-tenant hosts. Workaround: tighten max_batch_size for multi-tenant nodes during detected kernel contention.
4) KV-cache interplay: long tail probes often had lower KV hit ratio (due to partial prompt differences) which increased token-level costs; autotune steps that increased batch timeout sometimes made tail worse because KV-cache occupancy changed. We added KV-hit delta as a corrective signal to avoid perverse tuning.
5) Fairness: naive timeout increases to satisfy one service tier caused p99 regressions for other tiers. We implemented a simple penalty: reject tuning actions that increase the 95th-percentile ratio across tiers by >1.05. This kept fairness within acceptable bounds for our trials.

Representative run (mixed workload, probe_fraction=0.5%):
- baseline (no autotune): p50=9ms p90=22ms p99=108ms p995=190ms throughput=3200 req/s
- autotune enabled (after 4min): p50=9.5ms p90=21ms p99=98ms p995=130ms throughput=3160 req/s (1.25% drop)
- kernel time share: attention kernel rose 14% at baseline tail; after autotune attention kernel stayed high but memcpy reduced by 22% (less frequent tiny kernels).

Controller heuristic (current):
- On each 30s sample, compute smoothed p995 delta over 3 windows. If p995 > target + hysteresis and probe_ok, increment base_timeout += step_ms (start step 5ms, double on repeated triggers up to 40ms). If p995 < target - margin, decrement base_timeout by a smaller floor (step 2ms) to avoid oscillation.
- If kernel-contention-score > threshold (derived from kernel time skew), cap timeout increases and instead reduce max_batch_size by 10% increments.
- Use probe payload mix to sense whether tail is due to long input vs runtime queuing: long-probe triggered => prefer timeout increases; short-probe triggered => prefer max_batch shrink.
- Enforce fairness guardrail by checking tier-ratio before committing change.

What surprised us:
- Small timeout increases sometimes improved p99 but made p995 worse because they allowed a few enormous batches to form that blocked subsequent low-latency short requests. This motivated the hybrid approach (limit max_batch_size while nudging timeout).
- Probes that simulate multi-continue generation reveal different failure modes (KV eviction thrash) not visible from single-token probes.

Raw artifacts attached (links above):
- Flamegraphs: three sample traces (baseline, mid-autotune, post-autotune)
- CSVs: sliding-window metrics with probe markers for each run
- Kernel trace snippets: top 10 kernel names and their latencies
- Small script used to generate probe payloads: tools/probe-gen.sh (PR linked)

Next experiments (planned):
- Tune probe_fraction adaptively: start high after deploy, decay to floor when stable. Measure detection latency vs cost.
- Explore multi-objective reward (throughput cost per p995 improvement) using a lightweight bandit instead of heuristics.
- Try replica-aware tuning: do not tune nodes with >30% cross-tenant noise.
- Add synthetic KV-hit-preserving probe variants that re-play keys to avoid cache evictions while still exercising request-length behavior.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is the SLO for probe traffic from product? Acceptable overhead per cluster? (ask product/solutions).
- How to best communicate autotune actions to users (console events vs silent rollouts)?
- Need a way to correlate autotune actions with downstream cost reports.

Action items (short):
- PR to add KV-hit delta to telemetry (Evan) — PR #2145 in linked_artifacts.
- Add a short-run Canary that enables probes on 5% of pods for customer A traces (Marina + Priya).
- Draft a simple console readout for autotune actions and rationale (Samir).

Notes to self: keep probes unobtrusive, prefer conservative changes first, instrument everything. This file is messy by design — it's a living scrapbook. If something here looks actionable, copy to a new RFC and link back.

End of notes.
